A Conversation That Built a Model

Five months, one city’s school system, and a record of who did what

Adam Dennett FRGS FAcSS

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, UCL

Thursday 1 October 2026

Who I am, and why this talk

I am a Professor of Urban Analytics at UCL’s Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis. I build spatial models — of migration, of housing, of how people move around cities.

I am also a parent in Brighton & Hove, a city that spent 2024 arguing bitterly about which children should go to which secondary school.

I built the first version of that model myself, by hand, during the 2024 consultation. Two years later I rebuilt it with an AI collaborator — and it became something I could not have built alone.

This talk is about which parts were which.

This talk is not “I used AI to write my code”. It is an attempt to describe honestly what a research collaboration with an AI system actually looked like — with the receipts.

Part of the AI for Collective Intelligence hub’s interest in how AI changes the practice of applied research.

What exists now

The thing Scale
A strategic analysis of the city’s school system 9,712 lines of Quarto
A technical guide auditing every model term 4,736 lines
The model itself, plus data assembly ~7,400 lines of R
An interactive policy simulator (Shiny) ~3,000 lines
A private analysis repository ~8,200 lines
Three slide decks ~3,500 lines
Commits across six repositories 805

A production-constrained spatial interaction model with a competing-destinations term, calibrated per catchment, fitted against the council’s published offer data. It reproduces the September 2026 allocations with an R² of 0.95.

This did not start in April

October 2024. Brighton & Hove is consulting on redrawing its catchments. I write BrighonSchoolsSIM.qmd — 1,014 lines of R and Quarto. A production-constrained spatial interaction model of the city’s schools.

I call the hypothetical baseline Brightopia: where every child would go if distance were the only thing that mattered.

December 2024. I write bus_routes.qmd — 1,021 lines — setting up r5r, a GTFS feed and an OSM extract to compute real public-transport journey times to every school.

Two thousand lines of spatial interaction modelling and routing, written by hand, eighteen months before any of this.

That is what the new model was built on, not instead of. Brightopia is still in the current document, as the \(W_j = 1\) baseline the calibrated model is measured against.

I have been building models like this for twenty years. That is why I knew what to ask for.

The record I am drawing on

Claude Code keeps a transcript of every session: every instruction I typed, every action it took, timestamped.

For this talk I parsed ~250 MB of those logs across ten sessions, plus the git history of six repositories.

So the numbers that follow are counted, not remembered. They are also a snapshot — the work is still going.

1,277 instructions from me.

13,451 tool calls from Claude.

69 working days, spread over 166.

About ten and a half actions for every sentence I typed.

Five months, in one chart

Figure 1

The April–July work is a different project — a national school attainment model. The Brighton system model starts on 8 September and is finished eighteen days later.

What the 13,451 actions actually were

The largest single category is not writing code. It is running code and reading the result — the loop that turns a plausible script into a correct one.

The division of labour

What I brought

  • The working prototype — Brightopia, and the r5r routing pipeline, both written by hand in 2024
  • Twenty years of building spatial interaction models: knowing that attractiveness, distance decay and competing destinations were the terms that mattered
  • Knowledge of the school system, and of the city’s politics
  • Judgement about what is defensible to publish
  • Knowing when an answer was wrong
  • Every decision about what to do next

What Claude brought

  • Scale: a hand-built prototype turned into a calibrated, audited system
  • Data wrangling across a dozen published sources
  • Shiny, deployment, rendering, version control
  • Debugging, and the patience for it
  • Documentation written as it went
  • The willingness to redo all of it when one assumption changed

I knew what to ask for and what to examine, because I had built a smaller version of it myself. That is not a small part of why this worked.

What the instructions actually look like

Verbatim, from the logs. The counts are the tool calls that followed.

“fonts as well”

13 characters → 58 actions

“yes, build it”

13 characters → 46 actions

“yes, add Priory, Seahaven and Seaford Head as destinations”

58 characters → 68 actions

“Can you cite the sources and link to all of the data that is used in each section please then commit and push as I’m going to bed”

128 characters → 52 actions

Median instruction: 199 characters. About thirty-six words.

But the short ones only work if you know what to say

“You need to update Figure 28 with the new model outputs. Also, can I have a table of the original Brightopia (\(W_j = 1\)) model with the observed vs modelled expected numbers for each school”

“can I have a little section on how we arrived at the best \(W_j\) attractiveness factor — we end up using Attainment 8”

“can you just check whether the shared variance issues make a difference here? I don’t think they do, but it might be worth checking using the Shapley work”

These are instructions written in the language of the model. You cannot issue them unless you already know what \(W_j\) is, why it might be wrong, and what would count as checking.

The routing, as it actually happened

I was running r5r myself. It broke:

“Error in purrr::map(): Caused by error in checkmate::assert_class(): argument "r5r_network" is missing”

Then, an hour later:

“restarted R and re-ran, it’s routing now — we now have a brand new travel matrix — can we now go back to the original analysis and re-run the models with the new travel matrix? Both the public and private analyses”

213 characters → 35 actions

This is the collaboration in one exchange. I built and debugged the routing pipeline. It took the output and propagated it through every model, every document and every figure that depended on it.

Neither of us could have done the other’s half quickly.

Worked example: a school in the wrong place

The model had Hove Park School at its Nevill Road site. Reasonable — that is the address in the published data.

Five months in, I realised: the school has operated two campuses. Year 7 and 8 were at the Valley Campus, a mile away, until a closure proposal in 2026.

The model had been calibrated on the wrong location for the children who actually generate the demand.

No amount of code quality would have caught this. It needed someone who knew the city.

Re-calibrating moved about a quarter of Hove Park’s modelled intake between wards, and changed the disadvantage figures materially.

What re-calibrating it showed

Figure 3

Moving site is worth about twelve extra children a year — roughly a 7% lift, from geography alone. Real, but far smaller than the school’s attractiveness. The question “is it the site or the reputation?” now has a number attached.

Worked example: the simulator

Every scenario in this talk is a control in here. Built in about two days, and the reason the “what if” questions became cheap enough to ask twenty times instead of twice.

Worked example: a question only a human asks

Families choose schools on the published Attainment 8 score — which mostly measures the intake, not the teaching.

I asked: what if they chose on value added instead?

That is not a coding task. It is a question about how a city might behave differently, and it took about a day to answer properly: a new attractiveness basis, a switch in the simulator, a measure of how evenly children would be spread.

The answer: one struggling school’s intake nearly doubles, the surplus stops concentrating in three schools — and the total number of empty places does not move at all.

What the city would look like

Figure 4

Brighton Aldridge — the lowest Attainment 8 in the city — is adding more progress than almost anywhere. Patcham, comfortably mid-table on the headline number, is bottom of the city on value added.

Worked example: catching it being wrong

Claude reported a school’s value-added score as being in the “top 100% in England”. It had applied an Attainment 8 percentile function to a value-added figure. Silently wrong, confidently stated.

Later, the attainment charts appeared to show huge jumps when the value-added option was selected — because they were reading a different variable than I thought.

I caught both. It fixed both in minutes.

The failure mode is not gibberish. It is plausible, well-formatted, confidently-presented wrongness — exactly what a domain expert catches and a non-expert does not.

This is the strongest argument I have for why the human in this loop has to be someone who knows the subject.

The other failure modes, honestly

What went wrong What it cost
A shell quoting slip corrupted two files 20 minutes, fixed by regenerating
An optimiser fell into the wrong basin Caught by a sanity check on one school’s intake
A variable name collision inside the app Silent wrong behaviour until tested
Model outputs stale after re-calibration Needed a discipline of re-running everything
Confident summaries of work not yet verified Needed me to ask “did you actually check?”

None of these are exotic. They are the ordinary failure modes of a fast, capable, over-confident collaborator — and they are managed the same way you manage those in a person: tests, checks, and someone reading the output.

The workflow

Everything is Quarto. The analysis document, the technical guide, the slide decks — all .qmd, all executing live R against the same data.

The loop, many times a day:

  1. I say what I want, usually in two or three sentences
  2. Claude edits the source and runs it
  3. It renders, screenshots, checks the numbers
  4. It commits and pushes
  5. I read the rendered output and react

The document is the analysis. There is no separate “writing up” — changing the model changes the paragraph that describes it, because the paragraph is generated from the model.

Git is the memory. 805 commits, each with a message explaining why.

Why Quarto matters more than it sounds

When I asked “does the Hove Park change affect section 5.5?”, that was answerable — because section 5.5 is code, and the code re-runs.

When I asked for the deck to be rebuilt with the new numbers, no one had to re-type any numbers.

Reproducibility stops being a virtue you aspire to and becomes the only way the thing can work at this speed. If the outputs were hand-copied into Word, none of this would survive its own rate of change.

The recursion

The interesting part is not that it wrote code. It is the loop:

  1. A model produces a result.
  2. The result goes into a document, written to be read by councillors.
  3. Writing it clearly exposes a hole in the argument.
  4. The hole becomes a new question for the model.
  5. Answering it changes the model — and the document rewrites itself.

That cycle ran perhaps two hundred times. Each turn took minutes, not weeks. That compression is the whole story.

Eighteen days

Figure 5

What I would say to a colleague

It does not replace knowing things. Every moment that mattered in this project turned on domain knowledge I had and it did not.

It does collapse the cost of trying. The scenarios I tested would each have been a week of work. Testing twenty of them was previously impossible, so I would have tested two.

It writes better documentation than I do, because it never gets bored of writing it.

It needs supervision that looks like peer review, not like proofreading.

The bottleneck moved. It is no longer implementation. It is knowing which question is worth asking.

Open questions

  • Authorship. What is the honest way to describe this on a paper? I directed every step and verified every output — but I did not write the code.
  • Verification at speed. I can generate analysis faster than I can properly check it. That is a new kind of risk.
  • Reproducibility of the process. The code is reproducible. The conversation that produced it is not, in any meaningful sense.
  • Who else can do this? This worked because I could tell right from wrong. What happens when the person in the loop cannot?
